title: Question 2: Freedom to Gather in Places of Worship During an Emergency

context.text: Placed on the ballot by the legislature as Assembly Joint Resolution 10, passed by two consecutive legislatures (Assembly 56-43 on January 13, 2026; Senate 18-15 on January 21, 2026). The governor has no veto over constitutional amendments.

question.text: Question 2: “Freedom to gather in places of worship during an emergency. Shall section 18 of article I of the constitution, which deals with religious liberty, be amended to prohibit the state or a political subdivision of the state from ordering the closure of, or forbidding gatherings in, places of worship in response to a state of emergency, including a public health emergency?”

summary.text: The amendment would add to Article I, Section 18 (freedom of worship) the clause that the state or a political subdivision “may not order the closure of or forbid gatherings in places of worship in response to a state of emergency at the national, state, or local level, including an emergency related to public health.” Wisconsin Public Radio reports it responds to public health orders during the COVID-19 pandemic that limited large gatherings including at places of worship. No fiscal estimate was found.

measure.yesMeans: Amends Article I, Section 18 so the state or a local government could not order the closure of, or forbid gatherings in, places of worship in response to any state of emergency, including a public health emergency.
measure.noMeans: Leaves Section 18 unchanged; state and local governments keep whatever authority existing law gives them to limit gatherings in an emergency.

argumentsFor.text: Daniel Degner, President of Wisconsin Family Action: "Sadly, in 2020, we saw the government use emergency powers to abridge the people’s right to assemble in places of worship."

State Rep. Ron Tusler (R-Harrison), the lead author, in Assembly Judiciary Committee testimony: "This resolution doesn't ask for special treatment; it asks for equal protection. It ensures that the government cannot single out religious gatherings for closure while allowing other gatherings to remain open."

argumentsAgainst.text: State Sen. Chris Larson (D-Milwaukee): "None of us want to be in a position to prevent large, meaningful gatherings of our neighbors from taking place, and thanks to virtual meeting technology, we don’t have to. We do have a responsibility as government officials to preserve the lives of our constituents to the degree that we can. AJR 10 prevents public health officers from doing their jobs, endangering countless lives in any future pandemic."

League of Women Voters of Wisconsin, in its position filed with the Wisconsin Ethics Commission: "The League further believes that as public health crises increasingly reveal, a health program should protect the health of its most vulnerable populations, urban and rural, in order to protect the health of everyone."

Debra Cronmiller, executive director of the League of Women Voters of Wisconsin: "I think that conflating disease prevention with the right to worship is completely wrong-minded. No one's right to worship was compromised during that executive order period."

currentLaw.text: Article I, Section 18 of the Wisconsin Constitution currently provides that the right of every person to worship Almighty God according to the dictates of conscience shall never be infringed, that no person may be compelled to attend, erect or support any place of worship or maintain any ministry without consent, that no control of or interference with the rights of conscience is permitted, and that no preference may be given by law to any religious establishments or modes of worship or money drawn from the treasury for the benefit of religious societies or seminaries. It has no clause on emergency orders. The amendment would add the new clause to this section.

supporters.text: Wisconsin Family Action (testified in support of AJR 10 on May 7, 2025; says it will work with churches to turn out voters for the amendment)
Pro-Life Wisconsin (testified in support of AJR 10 on May 7, 2025)
State Rep. Ron Tusler (R-Harrison), the lead Assembly author, and State Sen. Cory Tomczyk (R-Mosinee), who testified for the resolution
Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor, who has said he supports all three amendments

opponents.text: League of Women Voters of Wisconsin (position filed with the Wisconsin Ethics Commission: "the League opposes this constitutional amendment")
State Sen. Chris Larson (D), who wrote that the amendment should be rejected
David Crowley, the Democratic candidate for governor, who has expressed opposition to all three amendments

researchNotes: Wisconsin publishes no state voter pamphlet with pro/con arguments, and the Wisconsin Elections Commission pages returned HTTP 403 to automated requests and were not bypassed, so the question text is taken from the enrolled joint resolution on docs.legis.wisconsin.gov, which states the ballot question verbatim (machine-checked; each enrolled resolution labels its question 'Question 1' because each was enacted separately). Official vote tallies are from the Legislature's bill history page. One argument per side was verified from primary statements (Wisconsin Family Action; Sen. Larson's press release). Other opposition (e.g., the League of Women Voters of Wisconsin and the Wisconsin Council of Churches, per Larson's release) was not independently fetched. WPR's voter guide confirms there are exactly three statewide questions on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot and their numbering. Added October 19, 2026: current law is the existing text of Article I, Section 18 as printed in the enrolled resolution. No official fiscal estimate and no registered-committee campaign-finance totals were found (the Wisconsin Ethics Commission's campaign-finance system could not be queried), so those fields are omitted. Group stances come from legislative hearing records, a lobbying position filing and WUWM, which lists groups 'including, but not limited to' those named. Sources disagree on the Wisconsin Council of Churches: Sen. Larson's release and the UW Law School State Democracy Research Initiative describe concerns or opposition in its statement, while WUWM reports it and the Wisconsin Catholic Conference registered as neutral, so neither is listed as supporting or opposing. The League's filing was found as a draft-style document with reviewer comments in the margin; only its stated position sentences are used.
